cultivar: Anhua and other Hunan medium- and large-leaf population bushes
processing: Grade-2 Anhua hei mao cha (pan-fired, rolled, briefly pile-fermented and dried over pine fires) is steamed and lightly packed into bamboo-leaf-lined baskets to dry and mature; not hard-pressed.
harvest_season: Late spring to early summer leaf, a bud with three or four leaves, slightly more mature than Tian Jian.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark-brown leaves, a little larger and more open than Tian Jian, with some stems, smelling of pine smoke.
appearance_wet: Dark brown leaves with visible stems, mostly whole.
taste_profile: Fuller and more robust than Tian Jian, with pine smoke, wood, dried fruit and a deeper sweetness from the stems, and a smooth, cooling finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, boiling water, short steeps; it also simmers well at 8 g per litre for 5 minutes. A clay pot flatters it.

vintage_note: Sold by year and factory in 1 kg and smaller baskets and loose packs, usually cheaper than Tian Jian from the same maker; market lots run 1–15 years and it drinks well from 2–3 years on, once the pine softens.
description:
Gong Jian, 'tribute tips', is the middle grade of Anhua's three loose basket teas, between the tender Tian Jian above it and the coarse Sheng Jian below. The name comes from the same Daoguang-era tribute story as Tian Jian; in practice it means grade-2 leaf – a bud with three or four leaves picked a little later in spring – which gives a fuller, more robust tea for noticeably less money.

It is made exactly like Tian Jian: the leaf is pan-fired, rolled, briefly piled and dried over pine wood, then steamed and packed lightly into bamboo-leaf-lined baskets to dry and mature. The slightly older leaf and the stems bring more body and more of the deep sweetness that stems give to dark tea, at the cost of a little of Tian Jian's delicacy.

In the cup it is pine smoke, wood and dried fruit with a rounder, sweeter body than Tian Jian and the same smooth, cooling finish; it gives eight or nine steeps with boiling water after a rinse and it simmers well, which Tian Jian does not need. Young, the smoke is forward; from two or three years on the sweetness takes over.

It is sold by year and factory in baskets and loose packs. Because the three Jian grades look similar once they are loose, the honest check is the leaf: Gong Jian should have whole but slightly larger leaves with a few stems, not the broken, stemmy look of Sheng Jian, and should smell sweet and smoky rather than dusty. It is the Anhua basket tea most worth buying by the kilo.

If you want a daily Anhua tea that still feels like leaf rather than brick, this is the sensible grade.
history:
Gong Jian is the middle of Anhua's three basket teas, with Tian Jian above it and Sheng Jian below. The history available comes mostly from the Baishaxi tea factory, the main maker, so read it with that in mind. By its account these lightly pressed basket teas appeared among ordinary people in the Qianlong era, and in 1825 the Daoguang emperor named the top grade Tian Jian as an imperial product. Tian Jian went to the emperor's own tea room, while Gong Jian and Sheng Jian went to the store used for gifts to princes, senior officials and tribal leaders. Treat the imperial part as the usual story.

The later dates are firmer. After 1949 the three were kept together as the "three jian" teas. In 1967, during the Cultural Revolution, they were renamed Xiang Jian No. 1, 2 and 3, Gong Jian being No. 2, and the old names came back in 1983. A Xiang Jian tea standard followed in 2009, and a national standard in 2016 with Baishaxi as its main drafter.
